brand.title: Brand

navbarShell.title: NavbarShell

authShell.title: AuthShell

userMenu.title: UserMenuButton

badge.title: Badge

hero.body: Auth, tenants, email and an AI agent — already wired in a typed monorepo. Clone App Base and turn the groundwork into your product.

stackSection.title: A stack you already know

foundationsIntro.title: Themes that recolor the whole app
foundationsIntro.body: Light and dark palettes ship with @app/ui. Pick a primary, extend with createTheme — the kit follows tokens, not hard-coded colors.

structureEnvironment.title: Configure. Run. Deploy.
structureEnvironment.body: One validated .env at boot, Docker Postgres and npm run dev locally, then render.yaml for production — the same knobs from laptop to Render.

structureBuild.title: Everything above is the template. Now build yours.
structureBuild.body: What you just walked is the model App Base ships ready — packages, env, database, storage, i18n. Your product starts when you add your own resources: a schema, a repository, routes and tools. The API page shows that pattern end to end with tasks — copy the folder, rename it, register it, ship.
structureBuild.cta: See how to add a resource
structureBuild.hint: Schema → repository → tools → DTOs → routes — then mirror it on the web.

tourIntro.title: See the product before you build it
tourIntro.body: Those foundations, rendered as real screens. Here's the tour, in the order you'd meet them: sign in, get set up, then step into the workspace and everything it ships with.

closing.title: From here on, it's your code
closing.body: This isn't a framework you depend on or a service you subscribe to — it's a starting point you own. Clone it and every line is yours: rename it, gut it, take it wherever your product needs to go. Even this landing page is just the first thing you'll replace.
closing.skipDemo: Or skip the demo — clone the repo and start building.

footer.builtWith: Built with React, Hono and Postgres

theming.title: Kit themes, brand when you need it
theming.bodyBefore: Light and dark palettes ship with @app/ui. The primary color drives buttons, highlights and focus rings; the rest is neutral surfaces. ThemeProvider writes CSS variables onto the page — the whole UI recolors with no component edits, no
theming.bodyAfter: classes to chase. Extend with createTheme when your product needs its own accent.
theming.tryIt: Try it — this page changes as you click. Your choice is saved and shared with the app.

i18n.title: Two JSON files, one t() call
i18n.body: UI copy lives in locale files — English is the source of truth, Portuguese ships beside it. Components never hardcode strings: they call t("…"), and the language picker (or the browser) does the rest. Add a key to both files and every screen that uses it updates.
points: en.json + pt.json under apps/web/src/i18n/locales/ — same keys, two languages
useTranslation() and t("tasks.title") — no providers to wire per page
Preference sticks in localStorage; first visit follows the browser language
This landing page is translated the same way as the app shell
i18n.tryIt: Try it — switch language here and the whole page follows, including this section.

database.title: Postgres, modeled in plain TypeScript
database.bodyBefore: Persistence is Postgres with Drizzle as the ORM — no separate schema language, no ORM console. A table is a
database.bodyAfter: in the domain that owns it. Identity, tenancy, the plan catalog, AI usage, articles, platform invites — then tasks as the example resource you copy.

resourceIntro.title: One resource, top to bottom
resourceIntro.bodyAfter: is the placeholder domain. Same name on API and web, fixed roles on each side, one shared contract in packages/shared. Walk the API (table → schema.ts → repository → route → tool), then the React domain (folder → api.ts → routes → page), and land on the screen. Copy that folder pair for your own resource.

environment.title: .env, local run, Render
environment.body: Validated env at boot, Docker + npm run dev locally, and one-YAML deploy to Render.

database.title: Postgres in TypeScript
database.body: Drizzle tables by domain — identity, tenancy, billing, usage, articles, and tasks.

storage.title: Files via MediaStore
storage.body: One interface for uploads — Cloudflare R2 in production, local disk when you skip credentials.

i18n.title: English and Portuguese
i18n.body: Locale JSON files and t() — switch language live and the whole UI follows.

monorepo.title: One repo. Workspaces, Turbo, one deploy.
monorepo.body: Everything lives in one npm workspaces + Turborepo repo: the Hono API, the React SPA, shared Zod contracts, and the UI kit. Turbo wires the task graph; render.yaml ships API + SPA as one service with managed Postgres.
points: apps/api, apps/web, packages/shared, packages/ui — one graph, not four repos
turbo.json defines the build/lint/typecheck pipeline across packages
render.yaml: one web service (API serves the SPA) + managed Postgres
packages/shared is the typed contract — change a shape, the forgotten side fails to compile

api.title: The Hono server
api.body: Domains own schema, repository, routes and tools. Cross-cutting pieces live in lib/, agent/, and integrations/ — never scattered.

layout.title: One folder per domain
layout.body: Open apps/api and the map is the product: domains/ for features, lib/ for infra, agent/ and integrations/ for cross-cutting work — never a grab-bag of files.

points: One folder per domain under domains/ — auth, tenant, task…
lib/ is pure infra (env, crypto, media) — domains import it, not the reverse
Agent tools sit beside the domain they act on
api.aria: apps/api folder tree in a VS Code-style explorer

web.title: The React SPA
web.body: Same domain names as the API. Each feature owns api.ts, pages, and routes — layouts and i18n stay in the shell.
points: domains/<name>/ mirrors apps/api/src/domains/<name>/
api.ts is the only network boundary for that domain
layouts/, i18n/, theme/ are shared chrome — not feature code
web.aria: apps/web folder tree in a VS Code-style explorer

ui.title: The UI kit
ui.body: App-neutral building blocks, grouped by role. Import per subpath — restyle through theme tokens, never hardcode colors.
points: primitives/ — shadcn buttons, inputs, dialogs…
shell/ — SidebarShell, NavbarShell, AuthShell, Brand
composites/ + theme/ — higher patterns and palettes
ui.aria: packages/ui folder tree in a VS Code-style explorer

config.title: One .env, validated at boot
config.body: Everything the app reads comes from a single .env, checked by Zod when the process starts — a missing or malformed var fails fast with a clear message. Only two things matter to run locally, and they already have working defaults; the rest are optional and degrade gracefully.
points: DATABASE_URL and APP_URL are all you need — both default for local dev
No RESEND_API_KEY? Emails print to the console instead of sending
No OPENAI_API_KEY? The AI agent is simply hidden — nothing breaks
SELF_SIGNUP_ENABLED flips the app between open signup and invite-only
PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS lists emails that are always platform admins once verified

storage.title: Object storage, ready before you need it
storage.body: Any domain that has to store a file — images, avatars, exports, whatever your product needs — goes through one small interface: put, get, has, remove. Add R2 credentials and it writes straight to Cloudflare's object storage with a public URL; leave them out and it falls back to the local disk, so there's a resource to build on from day one, not a feature you have to wire yourself.
points: MediaStore is the only interface a domain touches — swap the backend without touching callers
No R2 credentials? Falls back to the local disk automatically — nothing to configure to start
Images already run through it, compressed to WebP on write — copy that domain for your own files

localRun.title: One command, the whole stack up
localRun.body: No local Postgres to install: npm run setup uses Docker to boot Postgres 16, applies the migrations and seeds a demo workspace. npm run dev then starts the API and the SPA together — you're clicking a real app in under a minute.
points: Docker Compose runs Postgres on :5442 — nothing to install by hand
setup migrates and seeds a demo tenant and user for you
npm run dev boots the API (:5000) and the SPA (:3000) at once
The .env ships with working local defaults, validated at boot

render.title: Deploys to Render from one YAML
render.body: Production is described once in render.yaml: a single web service that runs the API and serves the built SPA, plus a managed Postgres. Push to main and Render builds, runs migrations on pre-deploy, and health-checks before going live — no deploy scripts to write.
points: One web service (API + SPA, one origin) and one managed Postgres
Migrations run automatically on pre-deploy, before traffic shifts
Auto-deploy on push to main, gated by a /api/health check
Secrets stay out of the repo with sync: false

delete.title: Delete the example
delete.description: Tasks are a placeholder. Remove the domain, drop the table, and put your product's resources in its place — nothing else breaks.

unsubscribe.title: Nothing to unsubscribe from
unsubscribe.description: Auth is scrypt and cookies, email is one swappable module, deploy is a YAML file. Swap any piece without asking permission.

rules.title: Rewrite the rules
rules.description: The conventions are markdown in .cursor/rules/, each scoped by glob to the files it governs — so the agent reads the same playbook. Disagree with one? Edit it, and it follows you instead.

convention.title: A feature is a folder on both sides
convention.body: Domain-driven development here is literal: one feature = one folder named the same on the API and on the web, each with fixed roles — not a grab-bag of files. The API owns schema, repository, dto, routes and tools; the web owns api.ts, pages, routes.tsx and components (plus context/hooks when it needs shared React state). Both import the same Zod schema and DTO from packages/shared, so a shape change breaks the side you forgot to update.
points: Same domain name on apps/api and apps/web — never scatter a feature
API roles: schema → repository → dto → routes → tools
Web roles: api.ts → pages/ → routes.tsx → components/ (context/hooks as needed)
packages/shared is the contract both sides compile against
Boundaries fail the lint, not just code review

schema.title: A table is a pgTable in its domain
schema.body: The tasks table shows the exact shape every table you add will follow: a uuid primary key, a tenant_id foreign key that scopes it to a workspace, the timestamps helper, and an index on the tenant. Run db:generate and the SQL migration is derived from this file — the schema stays the source of truth.
points: tenant_id ties every row to a workspace and cascades on delete
author_id references the user but is nullable — set null on delete
Migrations are generated from the schema, never hand-written

schemaFile.title: The pgTable that creates it
schemaFile.body: That table is declared in schema.ts with Drizzle's pgTable — id, tenant FK with cascade, optional author, fields, …timestamps, and an index on tenantId. Export the inferred Task type from the same file. Register the schema in db/schema.ts, then db:generate writes the migration.
points: Copy domains/task/schema.ts for every new tenant-scoped table
…timestamps comes from @/db/columns — don't reinvent created_at
Export from db/schema.ts, then npm run db:generate — never hand-write SQL

repositoryMethod.title: One method, one Drizzle query
repositoryMethod.body: Start here. A repository method is where the ORM runs — select, join, where, orderBy in plain TypeScript. list always filters by tenantId (isolation is not optional), optionally searches the title, joins the author, and returns rows. No hidden helpers; the whole query sits in the method.
points: Drizzle in the method body — this is the only place SQL lives
tenantId in every where — a missing filter is a cross-tenant leak
Returns DB rows / joins — not API DTOs yet

repository.title: Those methods live in one object
repository.body: Zoom out from list. find, insert, update, and delete sit beside it on a single exported taskRepository — fixed CRUD names, every method takes tenantId. Routes and tools call this object; they never write SQL. Mapping to the wire shape is the next step (dto.ts).
points: One object per resource: list / find / insert / update / delete
Same tenantId rule on every method you just saw in list
Callers stay thin — repository owns persistence

dto.title: Map rows explicitly — never spread a DB row
dto.body: dto.ts turns repository shapes into the shared TaskDto from packages/shared. Dates become ISO strings; password hashes and token hashes never leave the server. Routes and tools call toTaskDto — they don't invent response shapes inline.
points: Explicit field map in toXxxDto — never …row into JSON
Shared TaskDto lives in packages/shared — both sides compile against it
Dates are strings on the wire; secrets stay off the DTO

route.title: One handler, one action
route.body: Start here. A route file is a thin HTTP action — Input → Processing → Output. createTask validates with the shared schema, reads tenant and user from middleware context, calls the repository, and maps through the DTO. It never checks a session or resolves a tenant itself — that already ran on the group.
points: Handler sections: Input → Processing → Output
Tenant from context, never from the request body
parseBody + repository + toXxxDto — no SQL in the route

routeMap.title: Those handlers live on one group
routeMap.body: Zoom out from createTask. list, get, update, delete hang beside it in routes/index.ts — requireAuth and requireTenant once via .use, then one line per handler. Same aggregator pattern as the repository object and the tool array. Mount the group in app.ts under /api/tenants/:tenantId/tasks.
points: Middleware once via .use — every route inherits auth + tenant
One line per handler: .get("/", listTasks), .post("/", createTask)
Add a file, import it here, done

tool.title: One defineTool, one action
tool.body: Start here. A tool file is how the agent learns a single action — name, description, Zod input, and execute that calls the repository you already wrote. create_task reuses taskRepository.insert; tenant and user come from ctx, never from the model guessing IDs. The same definition powers in-app chat and remote MCP.
points: defineTool in one file — no MCP or OpenAI imports (lint blocks them)
execute reuses the repository — tools don't invent a second data path
summarize marks a write — it shows up as a chip in the chat

toolMap.title: Those tools live in one array
toolMap.body: Zoom out from create_task. list, get, update, delete sit beside it in tools/index.ts as taskTools — same role as the repository object for SQL. Spread that array into agent/registry.ts allTools and every surface picks it up. Add a tool file, push it onto the array, done.
points: One array per domain: export const taskTools: AgentTool[] = […]
Spread into allTools in agent/registry.ts
Mirrors routes/index.ts — folder owns its index

webConvention.title: Same name, different roles
webConvention.body: After the API half, the web domain for the same feature. api.ts is the network boundary; pages/ are route screens; routes.tsx exports the domain's <Route>; components/ holds product UI for that domain only. context/ and hooks/ appear when the domain needs shared React state — auth and tenant already do. Base UI (Button, PageHeader, EmptyState, useConfirm…) comes from @app/ui; there is no top-level src/components/ dump.
points: domains/<feature>/ — api.ts, pages/, routes.tsx; components/ with the first UI piece
context/<name>-provider.tsx co-locates Provider + useX; hooks/ for the rest
Product UI stays in the owning domain — never a shared components dump
@app/ui is tenant-agnostic; app/, layouts/, theme/, i18n/, lib/ are shell

api.title: One api.ts wraps every call
api.body: The only file that touches the network is the domain's api.ts — a thin object over the shared HTTP client, returning the same DTO the API sends. Pages never call fetch or the raw client directly, so every request for a resource has exactly one place to change. The tenant id is part of the path, mirroring /api/tenants/:tenantId/… on the server.
points: Network only through the domain api.ts — never a raw fetch in a page
Returns the shared DTO type — typed end to end with packages/shared
Path mirrors the API: /tenants/:tenantId/<plural>

webRoutes.title: Own your Route in one file
webRoutes.body: Each domain exports its <Route> from routes.tsx — one line for tasks, same pattern for articles, billing, account. The domain decides the path and the page; it doesn't know about the shell.
points: export const taskRoutes = <Route path="tasks" element={<TasksPage />} />
Same file role on every feature domain
No auth checks here — the shell already wrapped the tree

webRouteMap.title: Compose under the tenant
webRouteMap.body: tenant/routes.tsx mounts every domain under :tenantSlug and AppLayout. Drop a new domain's routes into that composition, add a nav item, done. RequireAuth and TenantProvider sit on the shell — pages don't re-check the session.
points: Compose {taskRoutes}, {articleRoutes}, … under :tenantSlug
Adding a feature = export routes + compose + nav link
RequireAuth and TenantProvider wrap the shell, not each page

page.title: Queries + chrome from @app/ui
page.body: Every internal page starts the same way: useTenant() for the workspace (TenantProvider — the React parallel to API middleware), useQuery keyed by the tenant for reads, then PageHeader / PageLoading / EmptyState so the page stays about the feature.
points: useTenant() — tenant from context, never parsed ad hoc in the page
useQuery keyed by tenant.id for every list/detail read
PageHeader, PageLoading, EmptyState from @app/ui — same chrome every page

pageWrites.title: Mutations invalidate; deletes confirm
pageWrites.body: Writes are useMutation with invalidateQueries on success — no manual loading flags. Destructive actions go through useConfirm; failures surface with showApiError(). Same shape for create, update, and delete.
points: useMutation + invalidateQueries on success — no local loading state
useConfirm() for destructive actions, never window.confirm
showApiError(err, fallback) for every mutation onError

screen.title: The result: a full CRUD feature
screen.body: That's the whole slice — API and web — and this is the screen it powers. Per-tenant create, list, toggle and delete, wired end to end through the shared DTO. Copy both domain folders, rename them, register the routes and tools, and your resource lands exactly here.
points: Per-tenant create, list, toggle and delete out of the box
The exact shape you'll clone for your product's resources
Delete the example and drop yours in — nothing else breaks

signIn.title: Login, clean and familiar
signIn.body: Email, password, a link to recovery, and secure sessions on submit — scrypt hashing and an httpOnly cookie, no auth vendor. Built with shadcn/ui, ready to rebrand.

signUp.title: Registration that sets everything up
signUp.body: Name, email, password. Each new user gets a personal tenant and a verification email automatically — the link is single-use and expires in 24 hours.

recovery.title: Forgot password, fully handled
recovery.body: Request a reset link by email, then set a new password on a screen guarded by a short-lived, single-use token — validated server-side and hashed with scrypt.

shell.title: A workspace, not a blank page
shell.body: Sidebar nav, a tenant switcher that appears only with more than one, a user menu and the theme controls. Your screens drop straight into the outlet.

agent.title: A chat that gets things done
agent.body: A floating assistant in every tenant: ask or command, it runs the right tools, shows what changed as a chip, and refreshes the data on its own.

account.title: Profile, security, and where keys live
account.body: Every user manages their own profile and password from My account. API keys for the remote MCP server live under Integrations — same patterns you'll reuse for any personal settings you add.

team.title: Bring the rest of the team
team.body: Owners and admins invite by email and pick a role; members and pending invites live in settings, each revocable. The invite lands as a 7-day link in their inbox. Seat caps from the tenant plan block invites when the workspace is full.

admin.title: Run the whole product from /admin
admin.body: Orthogonal to tenant roles: platform admins see every account and workspace (with members listed on each tenant), invite people to sign up for the app (their own workspace — not yours), assign plans, and bootstrap access with PLATFORM_ADMIN_EMAILS.

plans.title: Seats and AI entitlements, ready for Stripe
plans.body: Four plans in code — Free, Starter, Pro, and Pay as you go — with seat caps and per-member AI allowances. Platform admin assigns the plan; tenants see usage under Billing. Checkout later only needs to set planId. Wire Stripe or any payment provider when you're ready.

mcp.title: The same tools, over MCP
mcp.body: Mint a tenant-scoped API key under Integrations and plug the remote MCP server into Cursor or Claude — the agent's tools, right in your editor.

identity.title: Users, sessions and tokens
identity.body: The auth domain owns everything about a person: their credentials, the sessions that keep them signed in, and the single-use tokens emailed for verification and password resets. Passwords are scrypt hashes; sessions and tokens store only a hash, never the raw value.
points: users holds the account; a unique email is the login
sessions and action_tokens reference user_id and cascade on delete
api_keys are personal and scoped to one tenant for MCP access

tenancy.title: Workspaces and who belongs to them
tenancy.body: Every account works inside a tenant. tenant_members is the join table between users and tenants with a role, and tenant_invites carries pending invitations by email. plan_id on the tenant picks seats and AI limits from the code catalog — this is the backbone that makes the whole app multi-tenant.
points: tenant_members has a composite key of (tenant_id, user_id)
role is an enum — owner, admin, member — enforced at the type level
plan_id selects Free / Starter / Pro / usage entitlements (no Stripe required yet)
Invites expire and carry the role the person will get on accept

billing.title: Entitlements live in a code catalog
billing.body: There is no plans table. domains/billing/plans.ts exports PLAN_CATALOG — Free, Starter, Pro, and Pay as you go — with seat caps and per-member AI allowances. Tenants only store plan_id; platform admin assigns it. Wire Stripe later by writing the same field.
points: Four plans in code — edit the catalog when you fork
Seats + AI included vs passthrough, resolved by getPlan(planId)
Billing page reads the catalog + live usage — no payment provider yet

usage.title: An append-only spend ledger
usage.body: ai_usage_events records one row per assistant request: model, tokens, rounds, and cost in micro-dollars (USD × 1_000_000 — integers only). Spend aggregates per (userId, tenantId) against the tenant plan. The usage domain is ledger-only; the Billing UI is the face of it.
points: cost_micros never uses floats — micros keep money as integers
Scoped by user + tenant so seats and AI limits stay honest
No HTTP routes here — billing service reads the repository

articles.title: Articles with Markdown and a cover
articles.body: The articles table stores title, Markdown body, and optional cover metadata for tenant-scoped posts. Cover bytes live in object storage (local disk in dev, R2 in production) — the row is provenance plus the text.
points: tenant_id cascade; author_id set null on user delete
cover_path is the storage key, e.g. <tenantId>/uploads/<uuid>.webp
